subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Vision Zero
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Vision Zero.

hook.text: In 1997, Sweden announced a radical goal—zero deaths or serious injuries on its roads.

buildup.text: Most countries accepted some traffic deaths as inevitable. Sweden flatly refused.

discovery.text: Vision Zero redesigns roads, lowers speeds, and protects the most vulnerable users first.

twist.text: Sweden's traffic deaths dropped to the world's lowest even with harsh winter driving conditions.

climax.text: Cities from New York to Tokyo adopted Vision Zero, making zero deaths the new standard.

punchline.text: Zero deaths is a policy choice, not a fantasy.

quiz.question: Which country started the Vision Zero road safety movement?

details.summary: Vision Zero is a road safety philosophy originating in Sweden that aims for zero traffic fatalities by redesigning roads, lowering speeds, and accepting that humans will inevitably make mistakes.
details.whyItMatters: Vision Zero shifts responsibility from individual drivers to system designers. Cities adopting it have seen measurable drops in traffic deaths through redesigned intersections and speed reductions.
takeaways: The philosophy originated in Sweden in 1997
Road design absorbs human error rather than punishing it
Cities worldwide have adopted Vision Zero with measurable results

faq.question: Has any city actually achieved zero traffic deaths?
faq.answer: No major city has reached absolute zero, but Oslo and Helsinki have come very close with single-digit fatality years. Their success comes from lower speed limits, protected bike lanes, and redesigned intersections.

faq.question: How does Vision Zero differ from traditional road safety approaches?
faq.answer: Traditional approaches blame individual drivers for crashes. Vision Zero treats deaths as system failures and focuses on infrastructure changes like roundabouts and separated lanes that prevent fatal outcomes.
